analysis.one_liner: Slashes PAC contribution limits, bans soft money and leadership PACs, and gives a tax credit for small campaign donations.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, never got a committee vote, and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cut the most powerful special-interest money out of federal campaigns. It capped PAC contributions at $1,000, banned PACs from bundling checks from their members, banned the 'leadership PACs' that party leaders use to spread money to allies, and required political parties to report and limit spending on 'mixed' activities like voter drives — a ban on unregulated soft money. It also gave taxpayers a credit of up to $250 ($500 for joint returns) for small political contributions, and let local party committees spend unlimited amounts in congressional general elections. It required unions to get written approval from each member before using dues for politics.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, ordinary voters would benefit from a smaller role for PAC and special-interest money in elections, and small donors would effectively get their political contributions paid back through the tax credit. House candidates would be pushed to rely on local residents, since the bill barred accepting more from outsiders than from local individuals.

how_it_helps.text: Caps contributions from nonparty multicandidate PACs to any candidate at $1,000 total, down from the $5,000-per-election baseline, sharply reducing PAC leverage over House members. [S2] [S3]
Bans corporate, bank, and union separate segregated funds from acting as intermediaries or conduits bundling contributions to federal candidates. [S2] [S3]

Prohibits candidates from establishing or controlling leadership committees and bars principal campaign committees from donating to each other, cutting off two channels for laundering influence. [S2] [S3]

Subjects party spending on 'mixed political activities' — voter registration, get-out-the-vote drives, general political advertising — to the same limits and reporting as campaign expenditures, closing the soft-money loophole. [S2] [S3]

Gives individuals a tax credit of up to $250 ($500 on joint returns) for contributions to federal candidates and party committees, replacing big-money influence with broad-based small donations. [S2] [S3]
Bars House candidates from accepting more from people outside the district than from local residents, tying representatives to their own constituents' money. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the cost would fall on PACs — corporate, trade association, and union — which lose their favored channels and see their contribution cap cut by four-fifths; on labor unions, which could not spend dues on politics without written approval from each paying member; on big donors and party soft-money operations; and on the Treasury, which forgoes revenue for the contribution tax credit.
analysis.who_pays_short: PACs, labor unions, and big donors

drawbacks.text: The bill does not eliminate big money but reroutes it: local party committees could make unlimited contributions and expenditures in congressional general elections, and individual caps would no longer apply to party-committee contributions up to $25,000 a year, shifting influence from PACs to party machines. [S2] [S3]

The restriction on political use of dues applies only to labor organizations; no comparable written-approval requirement is imposed on corporate or trade-association political spending, so the burden is one-sided. [S3]
The tax credit is nonrefundable, so it helps only people who owe income tax and does nothing for the lowest-earning voters, and it costs the Treasury revenue that must be made up elsewhere. [S3]
Unlimited local-party spending invites circumvention, since money can be moved to whatever party committee the candidate's allies control. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core restrictions — a hard PAC cap, a conduit ban, a soft-money ban, and a tax credit for small donors — attack the same special-interest channels that dominated 1990s campaigns, and they outweigh the design flaws. But the bill's answer to special-interest money is partly to reopen an even wider door for party money, and the union-dues restriction is written to burden one side of the political spectrum and not the other. On balance a serious reform, imperfectly drawn.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees, neither of which ever took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lawrence Coughlin (R-PA) introduced the Campaign Spending Reform Act of 1991 on November 7, 1991. [S5]
The same day it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration and to the Ways and Means Committee. [S5]
Neither committee scheduled a hearing or markup, no further action was taken, and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PACs, labor-union and corporate political funds, party soft-money operations, and the incumbent members of Congress whose campaigns run on the existing money system are all better off because the bill never moved. Ordinary voters got none of the restrictions or the small-donor credit.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PACs and the existing campaign-money system

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only recorded support came from a single House Republican, and no member of either party signed on as a cosponsor.

industries.industry: Political action committees (corporate, trade association, and union)
industries.note: The bill cuts the PAC contribution cap from $5,000 per election to $1,000 total per candidate and bans PACs from bundling or serving as conduits for member contributions. PAC influence over federal candidates comes from exactly these channels, which is why reformers targeted them.

Unions lose both PAC channels (conduit ban, $1,000 cap) and a new rule barring any political use of dues or agency fees without a member's written approval, revocable at any time. Comparable written-approval requirements are not imposed on corporate political spending.

industries.industry: Political parties (national, state, and local committees)
industries.note: The bill bans party soft money by subjecting mixed activities like voter drives and general advertising to limits and reporting, but simultaneously lifts caps: local party committees could give and spend without limit in congressional general elections, and individuals could give up to $25,000 extra a year to party committees. Party organizations would become the main sanctioned channel for large campaign money.

industries.industry: Candidates and officeholders with leadership PACs
industries.note: The bill prohibits federal candidates from establishing or controlling any committee other than their principal campaign committee and bars campaign committees from donating to each other. Leadership PACs are a tool members use to bankroll colleagues and build influence, and this shuts that down.

industries.industry: Large out-of-district donors to House races
industries.note: House candidates could not accept more from people outside the district than from local residents, shrinking the pool of big non-local money in House campaigns.
